1051.title: Sirhind victory day
1051.hook: in May, Sikhs mark Banda Singh Bahadur's victory at Chappar Chiri
1051.tomorrow: The ninth Guru and his three companions
1051.howItsDone: Sikhs mark the victory at Chappar Chiri with kirtan, Ardas and langar, and some gather at Chappar Chiri, where the battle was fought.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the great holocaust remembered, and your line was they shielded the families. Did you stand between someone and a small harm? Today the calendar turns from grief to a day of victory, and it asks how a victory should be kept. Day one thousand fifty-one.

Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki Fateh: the Khalsa belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. On one early-summer day, that greeting carries extra weight on a field on the road to Sirhind. Kirtan rises, steam lifts from the langar pots, and the sangat sits down together. This is Chappar Chiri, where Banda Singh Bahadur's army met the forces of Wazir Khan, the governor whose order had ended the lives of Guru Gobind Singh's youngest sons. Sikh memory waited a long time for that day. Now the field holds a fair. Today: Sirhind victory day.
screen: `THE VICTORY IS WAHEGURU'S.` → `A FIELD ON THE ROAD TO SIRHIND.` → `CHAPPAR CHIRI.`

segments.voice: This path has already stood on this field, and walked into Sirhind with Banda Singh. Today, the question is how the day is kept. First, a wait that ended. In Sikh memory, the winter order at Sirhind was a wound that stayed open. When Wazir Khan fell at Chappar Chiri and the city was taken, that long wait ended. So the day is marked with joy, with kirtan and langar. Second, justice and revenge are not the same word. Revenge is about what I want back. Justice, in the Sikh telling, is about wrong being answered. The carry is not we got even. It's justice came, and the victory, as the Sikh greeting says, belongs to Waheguru, not to any commander. Third, the deeper court. In the Japji, Guru Nanak's morning prayer, the thirty-fourth stanza describes the realm of dharam, where, in paraphrase, each person is judged by their own deeds, and true is the One, and true is the court. On that view, no human victory is the last word. Banda Singh's day on the field is one answer; the true court is another. Fourth, the honest telling. Historians record that the city's people suffered when Sirhind was taken. A fair account of the day keeps that too. So the day is kept with joy, but it doesn't become a day to hate anyone living now. The boys in the tower aren't brought back by any battle. What came was justice, not repair. That's today's line: justice came.
screen: `A LONG WAIT ENDED.` · `JUSTICE IS NOT REVENGE.` · `JAPJI 34: JUDGED BY DEEDS.` · `THE HONEST TELLING.` · then, large: `JUSTICE CAME.`

segments.voice: Reflect on justice. Sit, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind one wrong you've seen, near or far, that hasn't been answered. It might be small: someone blamed for what they didn't do. It might be large. Hold it without anger for a moment. Then ask: what would justice look like here, not revenge, not getting even, just the wrong put right? You don't need an answer. Let the question sit with you. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, and leave the rest to the true court. The bell holds the time.
Sirhind victory day. The day each year when Sikhs mark Banda Singh Bahadur's victory at Chappar Chiri, when a long wait for justice ended. Today's word.
Your line: justice came. Today, set one small thing right that you got wrong: an apology owed, a credit you took that wasn't yours. Day one thousand fifty-one.

1052.title: The ninth Guru and his three companions
1052.word: The ninth Guru and his three com
1052.hook: Mati Das, Sati Das and Dayala are remembered with Guru Tegh Bahadur each year
1052.howItsDone: On the remembrance of Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, Sikhs gather for kirtan and Ardas, including at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, and remember Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala with him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sirhind victory day, and your line was justice came. Did you set one small thing right? Today, a day of memory that keeps a Guru and his friends together. Day one thousand fifty-two.

Strength is gone. I'm bound in chains. Nothing I do can help. That's the sense of a short salok of Guru Tegh Bahadur near the end of the Guru Granth Sahib, and tradition links it to his imprisonment, before his death in Delhi. But he wasn't alone in that prison. Three men had come with him, and they were put to death before him, tradition says, to break him. Each year, when Sikhs remember the ninth Guru, those three names are said beside his. Today: the ninth Guru and his three companions.
screen: `STRENGTH IS GONE. BOUND IN CHAINS.` → `HE WASN'T ALONE.` → `THREE NAMES BESIDE HIS.`

segments.voice: First, the names. Bhai Mati Das. His brother, Bhai Sati Das. And Bhai Dayala. This path met them in the story of Delhi: two brothers and a third companion, all close to the Guru. None of them was a Guru. Tradition says each was offered his life if he gave up his faith, and each refused. Second, how they're kept. When Sikhs mark Guru Tegh Bahadur's martyrdom, in gurdwaras and at Gurdwara Sis Ganj in Delhi, the three companions are remembered on the same day, beside him. The day isn't the Guru's alone. It's a Guru and his friends. Third, the salok and its answer. In the salok from today's opening, on Ang 1429, the ninth Guru says strength is gone and the chains are on, and then turns: now only the Lord is my support. The very next salok answers it: strength has come, the chains are broken, everything is possible, everything is in your hands. Tradition holds that this answer came from his son, Guru Gobind Singh, though readers differ on who wrote it. Either way, the two saloks sit side by side, like a conversation across a prison wall. Fourth, why three names and not one. A remembrance that kept only the leader would lose the people who stood next to him. Sikh memory keeps the companions in the light too. In the story, the Guru was not alone in the worst room of his life, and the day doesn't let anyone forget who was there with him. That's today's line: three companions.
screen: `THREE NAMES, NONE OF THEM GURUS.` · `REMEMBERED ON THE SAME DAY.` · `CHAINS, AND THE ANSWER: ANG 1429.` · `NOT THE LEADER ALONE.` · then, large: `THREE COMPANIONS.`

segments.voice: Say three names. Set out three small things in a row: three stones, three coins, three cups, whatever is near. With the first, say the name Mati Das, aloud or inside. With the second, Sati Das. With the third, Dayala. Then sit with all three in front of you and breathe slowly. Let them stand, too, for the people who have stood beside you in a hard room. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
The ninth Guru and his three companions. Guru Tegh Bahadur, remembered each year with Bhai Mati Das, Bhai Sati Das and Bhai Dayala, who would not give up their faith. Today's word.
screen: `THE NINTH GURU AND HIS THREE COMPANIONS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: three companions. Today, thank one person who stood by you when things were hard. A message is enough. Name what they did. Day one thousand fifty-two.

1053.title: The Sahibzade week
1053.hook: late December, Sikhs remember all four sons and Mata Gujri, some sleeping on the floor
1053.howItsDone: In late December, Sikhs remember the Sahibzade and Mata Gujri with kirtan, langar and the Shaheedi Jor Mela at Fatehgarh Sahib. Some families keep the week simply at home: no celebrations, and sleeping on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ninth Guru and his three companions, and your line was three companions. Did you thank someone who stood by you? Today, the remembrance moves to the Guru's own family, in the cold of winter. Day one thousand fifty-three.

In some Sikh homes in late December, the mattress comes off the bed and goes onto the floor. A thin blanket. The heater turned down. This is how the week before the new year looks there. No parties. No sweets. Children who'd normally be counting down to a holiday are told a story instead, the same story, night after night. It's the week Sikhs remember the Sahibzade, the sons of Guru Gobind Singh, and their grandmother, Mata Gujri. Today: the Sahibzade week.
screen: `A MATTRESS ON THE FLOOR.` → `NO PARTIES, NO SWEETS.` → `THE SAME STORY, NIGHT AFTER NIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, who the week keeps. Sahibzade means the sons of the Guru's house, and this week keeps all four of them together with their grandmother. Earlier this path told their stories one by one. Today, look at them side by side. Second, two places in one winter. The elder sons, Ajit Singh and Jujhar Singh, fell fighting at Chamkaur. The younger sons, Zorawar Singh and Fateh Singh, were held with Mata Gujri in the cold tower at Sirhind, refused to give up their faith, and were put to death. Tradition says their grandmother died in the tower. So the week holds a battlefield and a tower, both in the same cold season. At Fatehgarh Sahib the Shaheedi Jor Mela gathers crowds; at home, the week is quieter. Third, a song from that winter. Tradition says that after Chamkaur, alone in the forest of Machhiwara, Guru Gobind Singh composed a short song to the beloved friend, kept in the Dasam Granth. One line says, in paraphrase, that a bed of straw with the friend is good, and living in comfortable homes without him is like living in a furnace. The Guru, having lost so much, chooses the hard ground with the friend over comfort without him. Fourth, why the floor. Families who sleep on the floor this week aren't punishing themselves. They're keeping company: with a grandmother and two boys in a cold tower, with a father sleeping rough in a forest. For a few nights, their comfort steps aside so the memory has room. That's today's line: the cold week.
screen: `FOUR SONS AND A GRANDMOTHER.` · `CHAMKAUR, AND THE COLD TOWER.` · `A STRAW BED WITH THE FRIEND.` · `WHY THE FLOOR?` · then, large: `THE COLD WEEK.`

segments.voice: Sleep simply one night. Here's the invitation, for whenever you choose. Some night this week, give up one comfort before you sleep: a lighter blanket, a mat on the floor, no screen in bed, the heater lower. Nothing harmful, nothing extreme. For now, sit and breathe, and choose which comfort it will be. Then, sitting here, feel the floor or the chair under you. Let it hold you. Breathe slowly, and remember the four boys and their grandmother for a minute. If you pray, you can say Waheguru for them. The bell holds the time.
The Sahibzade week. The late-December days when Sikhs remember the four sons of Guru Gobind Singh and Mata Gujri, some families sleeping simply, on the floor. Today's word.
Your line: the cold week. Today, when you reach for a small comfort, pause once and let it wait a minute. Use the minute to remember someone who went without. Day one thousand fifty-three.

1054.title: Maghi: the torn letter
1054.hook: at Muktsar the story of the forty and their torn letter is told again
1054.howItsDone: On Maghi, Sikhs gather at Sri Muktsar Sahib to bathe in the pool, visit the town's gurdwaras and hear kirtan, and the story of the Chali Mukte and the torn disclaimer is retold. Gurdwaras elsewhere also remember them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sahibzade week, and your line was the cold week. Did you let one comfort wait a minute? Today, the calendar moves into the new year, and a winter fair keeps a story about a piece of paper. Day one thousand fifty-four.

The sound of paper tearing is small. A quick rip, and it's done. But Sikh memory has kept one tear for a very long time. At Muktsar, in Punjab, on the winter day called Maghi, crowds come to the pool and the gurdwaras of the town, and the story is told again: Sikhs who signed a paper walking away from their Guru, then came back and fell in battle, and the Guru who tore that paper up. Today: Maghi, the torn letter.
screen: `A SMALL SOUND.` → `CROWDS AT MUKTSAR.` → `THE STORY TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: This path has told the story, and walked through the Maghi fair. Today, hold the paper itself. First, a paper that said goodbye. During the siege of Anandpur, tradition says, a band of Sikhs asked to go home, and the Guru asked them to write it down. They signed a disclaimer, the bedava: you are not our Guru, we are not your Sikhs. A paper is a record. It can outlast the mood that wrote it. Second, the tear. Shamed and stirred by Mai Bhago, the same men rode back and fell at Khidrana, defending the Guru. Tradition says one of them, Mahan Singh, was still alive when the Guru reached him, and asked for one thing: tear up the paper. The Guru tore it. The record was gone. The relationship was whole. The Ardas names them as the Chali Mukte, the liberated ones, and tradition ties the town's name, Muktsar, to them. Third, a salok that says why it matters. On Ang 1372, Bhagat Kabir says, in paraphrase, that where there is wisdom there is dharam, where there is falsehood there is sin, where there is greed there is death, and where there is forgiveness, there is the Lord himself. On that reading, the Guru's tear wasn't a small kindness at the end of a battle. It was the Lord's own presence in a torn page. Fourth, what Maghi keeps. Maghi could have been a day about loyalty, about the ones who never left. Instead, the story it tells again is about people who left, came back, and were forgiven. That's today's line: the letter torn.
screen: `A PAPER THAT SAID GOODBYE.` · `THE GURU TORE IT.` · `WHERE THERE IS FORGIVENESS.` · `MAGHI KEEPS THE TEAR.` · then, large: `THE LETTER TORN.`

segments.voice: Tear up an old grudge. Take a scrap of paper, a receipt, a sticky note, anything. Write a word or two that stands for an old grudge you've kept: a name, a date, a single word. Nobody will see it. Hold it for a breath. Then tear it, slowly, in half, and in half again. You don't have to feel finished with it. Tearing the paper is only a start. Set the pieces aside, sit back, and breathe slowly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru. The bell holds the time.
Maghi. The winter day when crowds gather at Muktsar, and the story of the torn paper is told again: those who walked away, came back, and were forgiven. Today's word.
Your line: the letter torn. Today, delete one old message you keep rereading because it still stings. Let the record go. Day one thousand fifty-four.

1055.title: Hola: the Nihang parade
1055.hook: the Nihang dals ride and display gatka at Anandpur
1055.howItsDone: At Hola Mohalla in Anandpur Sahib, Nihang Singh dals ride in procession with horses and flags, display horsemanship and gatka, and the gathering includes kirtan and langar.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Maghi, and your line was the letter torn. Did you let one old record go? Today the calendar turns to spring, and to a loud, happy day of memory. Day one thousand fifty-five.

Hooves on hard ground, and a roar from the crowd. A rider in deep blue leans out of the saddle at a gallop and lifts something from the dirt with the tip of a spear. Behind him come more riders, tall turbans, flags snapping on long poles, drums. On the edge of the field, two young men circle each other with sticks and small shields, laughing between blows. This is Anandpur Sahib at Hola Mohalla, and the riders are the Nihang Singhs. Today: Hola, the Nihang parade.
screen: `HOOVES AND A ROAR.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.` → `ANANDPUR SAHIB.`

segments.voice: Earlier this path met Hola Mohalla, gatka and the Nihangs, each on its own day. Today, look at the parade as a day of memory. First, the dals ride out. The Nihang Singhs are organized in bands called dals, and at Hola they come to Anandpur with their horses, their flags and their old weapons, and ride in procession through the town and out onto the open ground. Second, a parade, not a war. Tradition says Guru Gobind Singh called the Sikhs together at Anandpur for drills and mock battles, turning the spring season of Holi toward courage. The Nihangs keep that memory alive the way it was given: as play with a purpose. The horsemanship is real and the skill is hard won, but the mood is a festival, not a threat. Third, gatka in the dust. Pairs spar with stick and shield, footwork first, eyes on the partner. Children watch and copy. A skill that could have been lost is passed on in public, in joy. Fourth, a prayer Sikhs sing with the same spirit. In the Dasam Granth, in a hymn often sung as Deh Shiva, Guru Gobind Singh asks, in paraphrase, for one boon: that he never turn back from doing good. It's a prayer for courage, and Sikhs sing it at gatherings. The parade gives that prayer a body: people who ride forward, not back, and who do it laughing. Memory doesn't always have to be quiet. Sometimes it gallops. That's today's line: ride in joy.
screen: `THE DALS RIDE OUT.` · `A PARADE, NOT A WAR.` · `GATKA, PASSED ON IN PUBLIC.` · `DEH SHIVA: NEVER TURN BACK.` · then, large: `RIDE IN JOY.`

segments.voice: Move with energy. If you're able, stand up. Shake out your hands, then your arms, then your shoulders. March in place for a few steps, lifting your knees a little higher than feels normal. Let it be a bit silly. If you can, smile while you do it. Then, still standing, take three strong breaths in through the nose and out through the mouth. Sit down, and feel your heart going. If you pray, you can say Waheguru with each breath as it slows. Notice that joy and strength can sit in the same body. The bell holds the time.
Hola. The spring days at Anandpur Sahib when the Nihang dals ride in procession and gatka is played in public, memory kept in motion. Today's word.
Your line: ride in joy. Today, do one hard thing with a lighter heart: take the stairs at a run, put music on for the chore you dread. Day one thousand fifty-five.

1056.title: Vaisakhi: 1699, 1919 and today
1056.hook: one day that holds the Khalsa's birth, a massacre, and a harvest
1056.howItsDone: On Vaisakhi, Sikhs gather in gurdwaras for kirtan and Ardas, celebrate the founding of the Khalsa with nagar kirtan processions and langar, and in Punjab mark the wheat harvest. In Amritsar, people also visit the Jallianwala Bagh memorial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hola, and your line was ride in joy. Did you do one hard thing with a lighter heart? Today the calendar of memory comes to a day that gathers several of this year's stories at once. Day one thousand fifty-six.

Three scenes, one day. In the fields, wheat falls to the sickle. In the gurdwaras, Sikhs sing the birthday of the Khalsa. And in Amritsar, some people stand quietly in a walled garden. Guru Nanak has a line in the Asa di Var that sounds strange on a festival: suffering became the medicine, and comfort the disease. Vaisakhi is a day that can hold it. The title of today's lesson carries two years and a word: the year tradition gives for the Khalsa's birth, the year of the garden, and today. Today: Vaisakhi.
screen: `THREE SCENES, ONE DAY.` → `SUFFERING, THE MEDICINE.` → `TWO YEARS AND A WORD.`

segments.voice: This path has spent whole days on each of these. Today, hold them in one hand. First, birth. At Anandpur, on Vaisakhi, Guru Gobind Singh called for those who would give their heads, and the five beloved stood up. The amrit was stirred, and the Khalsa was born. That's the first year in the title, the date tradition gives. Second, grief. On a Vaisakhi much later, troops fired on an unarmed gathering in Jallianwala Bagh, the garden this path stood in a week ago. That's the second year. Third, harvest. Long before either, Vaisakhi was the harvest day in Punjab, when the wheat comes in, and tradition says Guru Amar Das asked the Sikhs to gather at Vaisakhi. The harvest comes every year, whatever else happened. That's the last word in the title: today. Fourth, why one day can hold all three. In the Asa di Var on Ang 469, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that suffering became the medicine and comfort the disease, because when there is comfort, the One is forgotten. He isn't praising pain. On one reading, he's saying hardship can keep the One in mind, where comfort lets the One slip away. On Vaisakhi, the harvest and the birth are celebrated fully, and the grief is not pushed out of the room. Each keeps the others honest. Joy without memory would forget the garden. Memory without joy would forget the Khalsa's birthday and the wheat. So the same day holds kirtan, langar, processions, and, in Amritsar, silence in a garden. That's today's line: birth, grief, harvest.
screen: `BIRTH: THE KHALSA AT ANANDPUR.` · `GRIEF: THE GARDEN.` · `HARVEST: THE WHEAT COMES IN.` · `ANG 469: SUFFERING, THE MEDICINE.` · then, large: `BIRTH, GRIEF, HARVEST.`

segments.voice: Give thanks for three things. Sit, and breathe slowly. On the first long breath, bring to mind something new in your life, something just born: a friendship, a habit, an idea. Give thanks for it. On the next, something you've lost or grieved. Not to reopen it, just to honor that it mattered. Give thanks that you were able to love it. On the third, something that's ready, a harvest: work finished, a season you came through. Give thanks for it too. If you pray, you can say Waheguru after each one. Then rest with all three. The bell holds the time.
Vaisakhi. The day that holds the Khalsa's birth, the grief of Jallianwala Bagh, and the harvest, all at once. Today's word.

1057.title: Looking back: tellers and saints
1057.hook: Bhai Gurdas, the janamsakhis and fifteen Bhagats
1057.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the vars of Bhai Gurdas sung in kirtan alongside Gurbani, retell the janamsakhi stories of Guru Nanak at gurpurabs and to children, and sing the Bhagats' hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib as part of the Guru's word.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakhi, one day holding three things, and your line was birth, grief, harvest. Which three did you give thanks for? Today the year starts folding up behind us. Day one thousand fifty-seven.

Every story you've heard this year reached you because somebody told it first. A scribe bent over a page with a reed pen. A storyteller in a village courtyard, saying, and then Baba Nanak went on to the next town. A weaver at his loom, singing to God, whose song ended up in the Guru's own book. Before the battles and the kingdoms, year three began with these people: the ones who carried the story. For the last few days of the year we're turning around to look at the road. Today, looking back at the tellers and the saints.
screen: `SOMEBODY TOLD IT FIRST.` → `A SCRIBE, A STORYTELLER, A WEAVER.` → `TURNING AROUND ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: Start with the scribe. Tradition says Bhai Gurdas wrote out the Adi Granth in his own hand for Guru Arjan. He also wrote vars of his own: long poems in pauris, each with a picture and a point. He tells Nanak's journeys, the yogis on the mountain, the qazis at Mecca, the Guru laying down the pilgrim's robe to live as a householder. Tradition says Guru Arjan called those vars the key to the Guru's word. Next, the storytellers. The janamsakhis, the birth-stories of Nanak, came down in more than one family of tellings. The Puratan, the Bala, Miharban's reflective version, an illustrated one. They don't always agree on the details. Some readers take them as memory and devotion more than as diaries, and that is part of what they teach: a life so loved that people kept telling it, each in their own voice. Then the saints. Inside the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of the ragas, sit the hymns of the Bhagats. Kabir. Shaikh Farid, the Sufi. Namdev. Ravidas, who in his own hymns names the low caste he was born into and says the Name lifted him anyway. Dhanna the farmer, Sain the barber, and others. They came from many places, many castes, Hindu and Muslim backgrounds, and the Gurus set their words beside their own. One shape runs through all three: the Gurus' word didn't travel alone. It traveled in the hands of people who wrote, retold and sang it. That's today's line. The tellers.
screen: `THE SCRIBE: BHAI GURDAS AND HIS VARS.` · `THE STORYTELLERS: THE JANAMSAKHIS.` · `THE SAINTS: BHAGATS IN THE GURU'S BOOK.` · `THE WORD TRAVELS IN HUMAN HANDS.` · then, large: `THE TELLERS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the tellers. Sit comfortably and let the breath find its own pace. Then go back through the year and let one teller step forward. Maybe the scribe with his careful pen, or Bhai Nand Lal with his Persian verses of longing, or Kabir at the loom, or Farid, or the unnamed people who first said, and then Baba Nanak went on. Choose one. Your favorite teller. Hold that person in mind for a few breaths, and say their name quietly. If you pray, you can say Waheguru in thanks for them on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Looking back. Turning at the end of the year to see the road: today, the scribe, the storytellers and the saints whose words sit in the Guru's book. Today's word.
Your line: the tellers. Today, ask someone older for one story from their own life, and listen all the way to the end. Day one thousand fifty-seven.
